newsitem.title: USA: Clinton camp presses foreign policy in Florida.
newsitem.headline: Clinton camp presses foreign policy in Florida.

text.p: Even though foreign affairs has drawn scant attention in the 1996 election, the Clinton campaign on Tuesday began an eleventh-hour push to exploit U.S. policies on Cuba, Haiti and Israel in vote-rich Florida.

Campaign foreign policy spokesman James Rubin was sent to court Cuban-American and Jewish-American voters in Florida -- two key blocs that could help decide whether Republicans keep their recent hold on that state in presidential elections or President Bill Clinton wins it for the Democrats.
"Florida is a battleground state and we're pulling out all stops," Rubin, a former spokesman and top aide to U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright, told Reuters.

Pocketbook issues such as old-age health care programmes resonate loudly in Florida where the vote of seniors 60 and over is more significant than anywhere else in the country. But the state also "is one of the few places in this campaign where foreign policy can make a difference. The race (there) is still considered too close," Rubin said.

An independent poll published in the Miami Herald on Tuesday showed Clinton with an eight percentage point lead over Republican challenger Bob Dole in Florida. By that barometer, 47 percent of the state's voters favoured Clinton, versus 39 percent for Dole and eight percent for Reform Party candidate Ross Perot. Six percent were undecided.

Clinton campaign officials said their polls showed Cuban-American support for him at an all-time high but still below 50 percent. Jewish-American support for Clinton in Florida was substantial, they said.

But because the president has been perceived nationwide for so long as the clear frontrunner, his campaign is worried supporters will just assume he is going to win and stay home from the polls on Election Day.
Clinton is to make more campaign stops in Florida before the Nov. 5 election. He narrowly lost the state in 1992 and aides say winning it this time is a personal challenge.

Beginning Wednesday, Rubin will be on a five-day mission to make maximum contact with Jewish-Americans and Cuban-Americans in their synagogues and meeting places and on radio. He will concentrate on south Florida.
"These are two constituencies that care about foreign policy and vote," he said.

In his most significant Cuba-related move, Clinton overcame initial opposition to back the controversial Helms-Burton legislation after Castro shot down two civilian planes, killing four Miami-based Cuban exiles.

The law tightens the U.S. trade embargo on Cuba and imposes new sanctions on foreign firms doing business there. It has been immensely popular with strongly anti-Castro Cuban-Americans but has so angered European allies they have passed a retaliatory law.

Rubin said he would argue that Clinton has taken "all the responsible steps he could have to confront the Castro regime and try to convince the Cuban-American community they are as likely to get the success they want under President Clinton as under Bob Dole."
Many Jewish-American leaders including the American-Israel Public Affairs Committee have called Clinton the best friend the Jewish state has ever had in the White House, a point Rubin will emphasise.

Over the last four years, U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher has devoted more personal attention to trying to make peace between Arabs and Israelis than any other issue. But with the election of hardline Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu last May, Israel-Syria negotiations have collapsed and Israel-Palestinian talks have faced serious new problems.

Dole will be attacked as "no steady friend of Israel" and his record, including a call several years ago for a $3 billion cut in annual U.S. aid to Israel and his pre-Gulf War embrace of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein, will be stressed, Rubin said.

As for Haiti, Dole will be criticised for opposing Clinton's decision to send U.S. troops to the island as part of an operation in which a military dictator was ousted, a democratically elected president was restored, the way was cleared for new democratic elections and the flood of boatpeople to Florida's shores was ended, Rubin said.
